walkthroughs.body_html:
Geographical Debates — a core area of A-Level Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Geographical Debates brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Geographical Debates.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: John Snow's famous 1854 cholera map demonstrated that:
options: The outbreak was linked to a contaminated water pump
Cholera spread through the air
Cholera was carried by mosquitoes
Cholera was inherited genetically

mcqs.q: Food security is best defined as:
options: Reliable access for all people to sufficient, safe and nutritious food
A country growing all of its own food
Keeping large food stockpiles in warehouses
The availability of cheap fast food
Reducing greenhouse gas emissions to tackle the cause
Building sea walls against rising seas
Breeding drought-resistant crops
Raising the floors of flood-prone houses

mcqs.q: Can a single cold winter disprove global climate change?
options: Famines occur when people choose not to eat.
No — climate is the long-term average of conditions over about 30 years, while weather varies year to year; one cold season fits within a warming trend.
A record cold spell shows the planet is not warming.
Cold winters are caused by the Moon moving closer to Earth.

mcqs.q: Is famine usually caused simply by there being no food?
options: Famine happens only when a country physically runs out of food.
Famines occur when people choose not to eat.
Rarely — famines more often result from failures of access and entitlement: poverty, conflict and broken distribution, sometimes while food is still being exported.
Earthquakes only harm people standing outdoors.

mcqs.q: Do earthquakes and eruptions kill mainly because of their magnitude?
options: Famines occur when people choose not to eat.
The biggest-magnitude events are always the deadliest.
Not alone — death tolls depend heavily on vulnerability: building quality, warning systems, governance and wealth, which is why similar magnitudes kill very differently.
Earthquakes only harm people standing outdoors.

sequence.def: Set the aim and a testable hypothesis before any fieldwork
Use sampling (random/systematic) to gather data in the field
Organise into tables, graphs and maps (e.g. choropleth)
Apply tests like Spearman's Rank to find relationships
Answer the hypothesis using the evidence gathered
Assess reliability, limitations and how to improve the study
